_comment: Threats (docs/ADVENTURES.md §5.1, §8.3; world/threats.py): kinds of danger with a will behind them, made from what the history left. budget: how many may be stirring or active at once, by world size. near_hero: at most `untaken` of them within `tiles` of the hero that the hero has not taken on. start: at least `tier_one` tier-1 threats within `tiles` of a starting town (a week's walk is about 56 tiles). stage_days: how long a scheme's stage lasts, by tier. sign_lead_days: a stage's first sign comes at least this long before its effects. target_level: the party level a finale is measured for, by tier. tier_by_danger: [least danger of the home, tier]. wake: a dormant threat's weekly chance to stir by itself. emptied: a doomed settlement keeps `floor` of its people and comes back after `rebuild_days`. hunters: the history's beast-hunting heroes go on hunting (a weekly chance, more by fame). interlude_stages: the most stages a threat moves while nobody plays. A kind's creature: what its villain fights as when its figure has no creature of its own (the dead king risen, the gang's captain). A stage's roads: while its effects hold, bands of `group` are met more often (x `boost`) on the land within its reach - only at night if `night` - with these words as their coming (the dead on the road at night, the gang's men at the ford). A kind's ends: the world's own ending of it (a weekly `chance` while it stirs; its `outcome`; news from politics.json `text`).

beast.name: the beast
beast.ask: I hear something is killing your people.
beast.learn_ask: What does {villain} fear? What will kill it?

signs: Herders above {place} say something has been at the flocks again: whole ewes taken, the fences pushed flat.
In {area} they are finding sheep torn open and left, and tracks too big for any wolf, going up towards {home}.
A shepherd of {place} swears he saw {villain} on the ridge at dusk, and has not let his boys out since.
Dogs will not go near the woods below {home} now. The people of {place} have started to keep them in at night.
Charcoal-burners have left their pits in {area}: something circled the fires two nights running, and it was not hungry for bread.
flavour: Here and there along the track, tufts of wool caught on the thorns, and dark patches in the grass that the flies like.
A dead ewe lies by the path, opened and left. Whatever did it ate only the best of it.
Deep prints in the mud by the stream, and the bank torn where something heavy went up it.
The hens here are shut in behind new boards, and the farmer's dog sits against the door, shaking.
barks: Lost another ewe last night.
Those tracks were never a wolf's.
Count your flock twice, neighbour.
The dogs would not settle again last night.
Something has been at the fences.
overlay: They say they saw tracks on the road that morning, larger than any wolf's, and have looked over their shoulders since.
One of them asks whether you have heard of any beast in these hills, and watches your face while you answer.
They would sooner not speak of {home}, and glance towards it once and look away.
They mention that the dogs at the last place they stopped would not be quieted, and no one there could say why.

signs: {villain} has killed a man of {place}: a carter on the hill road, found in the morning with his ox beside him.
Two children of {place} went for firewood and one came back. They are saying {villain} is down from {home}.
{place} keeps its gates shut by day now. {villain} took a woman at the well, and nobody saw it come.
The bell at {place} rang all night: {villain} was among the houses, and a family is gone.
flavour: A cart stands abandoned on the verge, one wheel in the ditch, the ox's harness cut loose and trailing.
Scraps of a child's wool cap hang on a briar, and flies hum over the ground beneath.
A cross is chalked on the lintel of a lonely cottage, and the door behind it is barred from within.
Crows rise from the roadside as you come, and settle again as soon as you have passed.
barks: Keep the children in after dark.
Bar the door and keep it barred.
Did you hear it last night?
Nobody goes to the well alone now.
{villain} was in the lane again last night.
overlay: They ask whether you have heard of the killings hereabouts, and listen closely to the answer.
One of them makes a small sign over the heart whenever the trees close in on the road.
They mean to be under a roof before dusk, and say so more than once without being asked.
They tell you something took a person not far from here, and that the name whispered for it is {villain}.

intro: Wolves come out of the brush, thin and unafraid. They have been eating well off what {villain} leaves, and they have lost their fear of the road.
A grey shape lopes alongside in the trees, then another. The wolves of {area} have followed the beast's leavings down to the road.
Eyes in the dusk beside the track: wolves, grown bold on the leavings of {villain}, spreading to cut you off.

signs: Nobody walks the roads of {area} after dark now. {villain} has taken travellers within sight of {place}.
Farms round {place} stand empty, their people crowded into the village. {villain} grows bolder every week.
The lord's men went up to {home} after {villain}, and two of them came back. The country round is no one's now.
They are leaving the outlying farms of {area}. {villain} has the taste for people, the old women say, and will not stop.
flavour: A farmhouse stands with its door open and its hearth cold, the table laid for a meal nobody came back to.
The barley here is unharvested, going over in the wind with no one left to cut it.
Someone has nailed a row of sharpened stakes across a gap in the hedge, as though that would help.
A heap of picked bones lies in the ditch, and not all of them are a beast's.
barks: Don't go out after sundown. Not for anything.
We leave at the new moon, all of us.
My brother went to the high fields. Nothing since.
Sleep in the loft and pull the ladder up.
Whatever lives in {home} has found a taste for us.
overlay: They warn you not to be on this road after dark, and say they have seen what is left of those who were.
One of them says the country round {home} has gone quiet, no birds and no dogs, nothing at all.
They keep close together in the middle of the road, and start at every sound from the hedge.
They ask how far it is to the next place with a gate that shuts, and do not wait to hear the whole answer.

intro: The wolves are starving and past caution. They come at you in the open road, in daylight, with {villain}'s kills still on their muzzles.
A pack has been feeding on what {villain} leaves round {home}, and now it wants fresher meat. They circle you in the road.
Lean, hollow wolves spread out across the way, long used to men as meat since {villain} began its work.

signs: {place} is packing its carts. Whoever can walk is leaving before {villain} comes again.
Refugees from {place} are on the roads with what they could carry. {villain} has had the last of their patience and their kin.
The headman of {place} has given up: the village will be left by the next new moon, and {villain} can have it.
There is talk in {area} of nothing but {villain}. {place} cannot hold another month of it.
flavour: A line of abandoned carts stands along the road, left where their axles failed.
Houses with their thatch torn down for cart-covers, and the wells stopped with stones before the people left.
A gate is broken, and deep claw-marks are gouged into the doorpost at the height of a man's head.
Smoke stands over the valley, thin and black. Somewhere below it a bell is tolling and nobody answers.
barks: Leave it. Leave it all and walk.
Take the cart. We can buy another.
Mind the old woman, she's slow.
It'll have the place when we're gone.
Don't look back at the hill, love.
overlay: They say no one will be left in {area} by winter, and speak as though it had already happened.
They will not stop to talk, and ask only that you turn back, since nothing ahead is worth the going.
One of them says that {villain} cannot be stopped, and that those who tried are not spoken of any more.
They look back along the road more than they look ahead, and none will say what they expect to see.

hooks: {town} pays good silver for the hide of {villain}, that lairs at {home}, {where}.
Wanted: someone to put an end to {villain}. The people of {town} will feed and house whoever tries. It lairs at {home}, {where}.
{villain} has killed again. Anyone with the stomach for a hunt, ask for the headman of {town}. Its lair is {home}, {where}.
A widow of {town} will give everything she has to whoever kills {villain}. It sleeps at {home}, {where}.

risen.name: the risen
risen.ask: I hear the dead are walking here.
risen.learn_ask: Who was {villain}? What holds {him} in the world?

signs: Graves have been opened in the churchyard at {place}, from below, the sexton swears, not from above.
Every dog in {place} howls towards {home} at moonrise, and none of them will be called in.
A cold mist lies on {home} in the mornings now, and the shepherds of {area} keep their flocks away from it.
Lights have been seen going in and out of {home} at night, slow, the way a procession walks.
The old women of {place} are hanging iron over their doors again. They say the one in {home} is turning over.
flavour: A grave by the track has been opened. The earth is thrown outwards, as if whoever lay there dug his own way up.
The birds are quiet here. Even the crows keep off the barrow-ward side of the road.
Someone has driven an iron nail into every gatepost along this lane, and hung a sprig of rowan from each.
A cold patch lies on the road where no cloud shadows it, and the frost has not lifted from it all day.
barks: Heard the dogs again last night?
There's earth on the churchyard path.
Hang iron over your door, I say.
My mother said it would come to this.
They say {home} has been opened.
overlay: They avoid looking towards {home}, and one of them touches a bit of iron at his belt.
One of them says the ground felt wrong underfoot a little way back, and laughs as if it were a joke.
They ask if you have seen lights on the hills by night, and look no easier when you say you have not.
They speak low about a cold mist they passed through that morning, and break off when you come near.

intro: Figures stand in the road ahead, very still in the moonlight. They have been dead a long time, and they turn to you all at once.
A slow procession comes up the road from {home}, without lanterns, without a sound. The dead of {villain} are walking.
Bones in rotted mail climb out of the ditch as you pass. Someone in {home} has sent them for you.
The mist off the barrow-fields thickens round you, and there are shapes walking in it that should be lying down.

signs: The dead walk the roads round {place} at night. A carter swears he passed a whole line of them, going towards {home}.
Two men of {place} went out after dark and did not come back. Their tracks went up towards {home}, side by side with others.
Nobody in {area} travels after sunset now: things in old armour stand at the crossroads, waiting.
{place} keeps fires burning at every gate all night. The dead came to the fence and stood there till cockcrow.
They are saying in {place} that {villain} is awake, and has called his old guard out of the ground.
flavour: A line of bare footprints crosses the road at dusk, narrow, and all going the same way, up towards the barrow.
A black spear-haft stands in the verge, newly pushed up out of the ground.
Bonfires burn at the gate of every steading, and nobody sits near one alone.
A sword rusted to red crumbs lies in the road, as though its bearer forgot it.
barks: Keep the gate fire lit till cockcrow.
They stood at the fence again last night.
Don't answer if they call your name.
Salt on the sill, and iron by the bed.
{villain} is awake. You can feel it.
overlay: They say they saw figures standing at a crossroads last night, and did not wait to learn who they were.
One of them carries a lantern lit at midday and will not put it out.
They watch the shadows between the trees as if expecting them to move.
They tell you the dead are abroad by night in {area}, and that you should be behind a barred door by dusk.

intro: Some of the dead on the road wear the clothes of farm folk, and not long dead at that. They walk towards {home} and do not stop for you - until they do.
A woman in a nightdress walks barefoot up the road, her eyes open and empty. Behind her come the others, and they have noticed you.
A line of the dead goes by in the dark, old bones and new, all walking to {home}. The last of them turn aside for you.

signs: A hamlet near {place} woke to find half its people gone: beds empty, doors open, footprints going up to {home}.
Refugees on the road from {area} tell of their own kin getting up at midnight and walking out towards {home}, and not hearing when called.
The priest of {place} rang the bell all night, and still the sleepers went out to {villain}. In the morning there were only the old and the children.
There are new dead walking with the old ones round {home} now. People of {area} know their faces.
flavour: A cottage door hangs open, the bed inside still rumpled, and bare footprints go out through the dew.
A hamlet lies silent at midday, no smoke from any chimney, a cradle on its side by the door.
The churchyard grass is trampled flat in a path from the village houses straight up towards {home}.
Washing hangs on a line, three days dry, in a yard where no one comes to take it in.
barks: Old Wen's lad walked out in his sleep.
Hold the children's hands at night.
I saw her face. She did not know me.
Lock the doors from within.
Half the street is gone, and no one sings.
overlay: They look hollow-eyed and grey, as people do who have kept watch through too many nights.
One of them asks if you have seen anyone walking the road alone by night, and does not say why.
They keep a cord tied from wrist to wrist as they walk, so that none can wander off in the dark.
They say sleepers have been getting up and walking out towards {home}, and that they will not sleep apart tonight.

intro: Even by day the dead keep the roads here now. They come out of the grey light in their old ranks, as if the land were theirs again.
The dead of {villain} hold this road. They stand aside for nobody living.

signs: The dead are marching out of {home}, rank on rank, and {place} is in their way.
{villain} has come out of {home} in his old crown, they say, and his dead walk before him towards {place}.
There is no more sleeping in {area}. {villain} means to have the living country back, and {place} is the first of it.
Bells all night in {area}: the dead are on the march, and {place} is emptying ahead of them.
flavour: Rows of footprints cross the fields in good order, the wheat trampled flat in a swathe as wide as a road.
The sky over {home} is grey at noon, and the grey is spreading towards the road like a stain on cloth.
A village stands with every door open and every house empty, each road out of it trodden bare.
The rooks have deserted the trees. Only the cold wind talks in the branches.
barks: Run! Run for the river!
Leave the flocks. Leave everything.
They're coming down the north lane.
The crown. I saw the crown.
Gather the children. Gather them now.
overlay: They are in a great hurry, and point back along the road towards {home} before they say a word.
One of them says they saw ranks of armoured figures on the far hill at dawn, and not one cast a shadow.
They tell you there is no safe road left in {area}, and advise you to turn back while you can.
They make no effort to hide their fear, and ask only which way the road is clear.

hooks: The priest of {town} asks for anyone with the courage to go up to {home}, {where}, where {villain} has woken.
The dead walk round {town}. The headman will pay whoever puts {villain} back in his grave at {home}, {where}.
Help wanted at {town}: the barrow of {villain} is open, {where}, and the dead come out of it by night.
Families of {town} who have lost their own to the walking dead ask for someone to lay {villain} to rest. His barrow is {home}, {where}.

outlaw.name: the outlaw lord
outlaw.ask: I hear your roads are being bled.
outlaw.learn_ask: Who in this town sells {villain} the caravans' days?

intro: A rope is drawn up across the road from the ditch, and men step out on both sides. {gang} wants its toll.
A man sits on a fallen tree across the way, eating an apple. "Road's closed," he says, "unless you pay {villain}." His friends come out of the trees.
There are men waiting at the ford with crossbows, and a fire, as if they have been there a while. They wear {gang}'s rag on their arms.

signs: A carter of {place} was stopped on the road and stripped of his load by men who said they were {villain}'s.
{gang} has drawn a chain across the road below {place}, and takes a toll from all who pass.
Merchants in {area} have started riding in company. {gang} took two wagons in a week.
A pedlar walked into {place} in his shirt, with nothing else. {villain}'s men took the rest, his boots included.
flavour: A wagon lies on its side in the ditch, its load gone, its axle cut through.
A rag is tied round a milestone here - the gang's mark, the carters say: this road pays.
Fresh hoofprints leave the road here, many of them, and go off into the scrub towards nowhere honest.
A notched stick hangs from a tree beside the road, one notch for every cart that has paid.
barks: Another toll. We'll starve at this rate.
Pay them and they leave you alone.
The price of salt has doubled, mind.
Don't travel alone on the north road.
{villain}'s men were at the ford again.
overlay: They say there is a chain across the road ahead, and that men there will want a word with you.
One of them glances up at every ridge and tree line as they talk.
They ask which side you are on, and watch your hands while you answer.
They say the road is not what it was, and that you will soon see why.

intro: They are waiting at the bend, where the trees close in. {gang} has learned which roads are worth watching.
A boy runs out into the road shouting for help, and when you stop, his friends come out of the hedge with their blades out. {gang} sends its regards.
Horsemen come up behind you at a trot and spread out across the road. "{villain} says you're carrying too much," one of them calls.

signs: No wagon has reached {place} in a fortnight without paying {gang}. Salt and iron cost twice what they did.
The lord's toll-keeper on the road to {place} was found hanged from his own gate. {villain} does not like competition.
{place} sent to its lord for soldiers against {gang}, and the messenger came back without his ears.
They say {villain} knows every wagon that leaves {place} before it is loaded. Someone in town is talking.
flavour: A milestone has been pushed over, and under it lies a hollow where something was hidden and since dug out.
The inn at the crossroads is shuttered, its sign painted over with a red rag.
A man hangs from a roadside tree, a placard on his chest in a hand that can scarcely write.
Wheel-ruts turn aside from the old road into the fields: carters now go the long way round the bend.
barks: No wagon's come in for a fortnight.
Watch who you talk to in the tavern.
Somebody is selling our days to them.
They hanged the toll-keeper from his own gate.
{villain} has eyes in every yard.
overlay: They keep their voices low, and look at you as though weighing whether you ride with {villain}.
They say someone in the towns is passing word of who travels and when, and so they trust no stranger.
One of them says the lord's men have stopped coming this way, and nobody asks why.
They are anxious to be out of the open, and choose their words with care.

intro: Men ride out of the trees in a long line, and one at their head with a captain's sash. {gang} does not hide any more.
There are more of them than any robbers have a right to be. {villain} has been recruiting.

signs: {gang} rode into a village of {area} by daylight, took what they liked, and drank the inn dry before they left.
Deserters and runaways are going up to {home} to join {villain}. They say he pays better than the lord.
{villain} has sent word to {place}: a tenth of everything, every month, or the barns burn.
The lord's patrol met {gang} on the road and came off worst. Nobody in {area} expects another.
flavour: Horse-dung lies thick on the road, and the verge is trampled by many riders.
A burned barn stands at the roadside, still smoking at the beams, and no one has come to look at it.
An inn-yard is full of strange horses, and someone has scratched a crude mark into the sign with a knife.
Fresh graves lie in a row at the edge of a village, and a lord's torn livery lies on the nearest.
barks: They drank the inn dry and paid nothing.
The lord's men ran. I saw them run.
My son's gone up to join them, the fool.
A tenth, they said. A tenth or the barns.
Never seen so many riders on one road.
overlay: They talk of riders in numbers they never saw before, and keep a nervous eye on the wood.
One of them says men are going up to {home} to join {villain}, and that it spreads like a fever.
They say a patrol went by that morning and came back wounded, or did not come back.
They ask whether you have heard of anyone standing against {villain}, and seem to doubt it.

signs: {place} has given in. Every month a cart goes up to {home} with a tenth of all they have, and {villain} lets them live.
The headman of {place} has sworn to {villain} on the green, with the gang's riders round him. The town pays now.
{gang} rules the roads of {area}. {place} pays its tribute, and the lord does nothing.
There is a new law in {place}, and it is {villain}'s: pay, and keep your roof.
flavour: A tithe-cart rolls along the road under guard, piled high, its driver not looking at anyone.
A new post stands at the village edge, painted in the gang's colour, with a pole across the road.
Every door in the lane bears the same chalk mark: paid this month.
The lord's banner hangs from the village gate, upside down and mouldering, and no one has taken it down.
barks: Pay and keep your roof, that's the law.
Tithe day tomorrow. Count the barley.
Say nothing in front of the riders.
It could be worse. It will be.
{villain}'s law is the only law now.
overlay: They say the road is safe now if you know whom to pay, and the way they say it is no comfort.
They are polite and wary, and quick to name {villain} as the one who keeps order here.
They offer no trouble and ask for none, with the flat look of people long past arguing.
One of them says it is wiser not to ask what the law is in {area}, only to learn it.

hooks: The merchants of {town} will pay well for the end of {villain} and {gang}, that hold the roads from {home}, {where}.
Wanted, alive or otherwise: {villain}, captain of {gang}. Ask at the gate of {town}. The gang keeps to {home}, {where}.
{town} has had enough of paying {gang}. Whoever breaks {villain} at {home}, {where}, will want for nothing here.
A robbed carter of {town} offers all he has left to whoever brings down {villain}. His men lie up at {home}, {where}.
